Introduction to Internet

### Page 23
What is internet?
Origin: The Internet began in 1969 as ARPANET, a project of the U.S.
Department of Defense.
Purpose: Designed to withstand major disasters using a decentralized
network structure.
Definition: A network of networks using standardized protocols (TCP/IP),
allowing communication between millions of computers worldwide.
Growth:
•Initially limited to government, military, and academic use.
•Expanded in the 1990s to include entertainment, communication, and e-commerce.
•By 2002, over 600 million users worldwide.
Modern Structure:
•Decentralized with independently owned networks.
•Large, high-speed networks = backbone providers.
•ISPs (Internet Service Providers) lease bandwidth from backbones and provide
access to users.

### Page 24
History of Internet - Key
Milestones
• 1950s: Initiated during the Cold War to connect top US universities via the Advanced
Research Projects Agency (ARPA).
• 1969: ARPANET established successful computer communication.
• 1971: Ray Tomlinson invented email.
• 1973: TCP/IP protocols and Ethernet emerged.
• 1982: TCP/IP was made mandatory by the US Defense Department; term "Internet"
was coined.
• 1984: Domain Name System (DNS) introduced.
• 1988: First major computer worm attack led to the creation of CERT.
• 1989-1991: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web (WWW) and introduced
the first web browser.
• 1993: Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina developed Mosaic, the first popular graphical
web browser.

### Page 25
History of Internet - Key
Milestones
• 1994: Netscape Communications founded; Netscape Navigator browser released.
• 1995: Internet Explorer 1.0 launched by Microsoft.
• 1998: Google founded, revolutionizing web search.
• 2004: Web 2.0 popularized with emphasis on user-generated content and
interactivity.
• 2007: Apple iPhone released, initiating mobile web revolution.
• 2010s: Rise of cloud computing, responsive design, and progressive web apps.
• 2020s: Continued growth of AI, voice search, and immersive technologies like AR/VR
on the web.

### Page 31
Domain Name
Domain names are your online address, essential for guiding people to
your website, facilitating seamless access to websites and content.
What is a Domain Name?
A domain name is a distinctive, human-readable web address that
substitutes complex numerical IP addresses. For example, nytimes.com
is the domain name that directs users to The New York Times’ website.
These identifiers:
• Simplify access to websites
• Improve brand recognition
• Enhance user experience
• Serve as unique identifiers in the digital space

### Page 54
Introduction to HTML
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.
• It is used to create web pages and hypertext documents.
• HTML is a markup language, not a programming language.
• It specifies the structure and format of web content using tags.
• Hypertext enables users to jump between sections or documents instead of following a
linear reading flow.
• Platform Independence
• HTML is platform-independent: any device with an internet browser can view HTML
content, regardless of operating system.
• Web browsers act as HTML formatters, rendering content based on tags and platform
capabilities.
Elements and Tags
• HTML tags label parts of content (e.g., paragraphs, headings).
• Content outside tags is rendered directly on the browser.
• HTML does not define font style or layout directly; appearance may vary across platforms.
Advantages of HTML
• Small file size due to absence of styling information.
• Cross-platform and device independent.
• Requires only a browser to view content.
• Easy to create and share documents over the internet.

### Page 110
DHTML
DHTML is Dynamic Hypertext Markup Language.
DHTML is not a language itself, but rather a combination of
technologies like HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, that are used
together to create dynamic and interactive web pages.
• HTML (HyperText Markup Language): Provides the basic structure
and content of the web page.
• CSS (Cascading Style Sheets): Used to control the visual
presentation and layout of the page.
• JavaScript: Adds interactivity and dynamic behavior to the page,
allowing it to respond to user actions and update content without
requiring a full page reload.
• DOM (Document Object Model): Provides a programming
interface for HTML elements, allowing JavaScript to access and
manipulate the page's content and structure.

Opacity
CSS Opacity in Firefox, Safari, Chrome, Opera and IE9
Here is the most up to date syntax for CSS opacity in all current browsers.
Example »
p {
opacity: 0.7;
}
The above style rule will make the paragraph element 70% opaque (or
30% transparent).
The opacity property takes a value a value from 0.0 to 1.0. A setting of
opacity: 1; would make the element completely opaque (i.e. 0%
transparent), whereas opacity: 0; would make the element completely
transparent (i.e. 100% transparent).

title: WAD - Web Application Development Syllabus & Lab Policies

chunks.content: Web Application Development (WAD) is instructed by Prof. AD. Theory lectures take place in Room 402/403. Elective laboratory sessions: Batch C1 is scheduled on Thursdays 02:10 PM - 04:00 PM in Lab 4B; Batch C2 is on Fridays 03:10 PM - 05:00 PM in Lab 3A. Focus areas include Full-Stack JavaScript, React 19, Node.js, Express, and MongoDB vector search.

WAD Semester 5 evaluation criteria: Laboratory Practical Implementation & Viva: 30%, Midterm Assessment: 25%, End-Semester Full Stack Project: 25%, Continuous Quizzes & Mini-Assignments: 20%. Minimum score required for passing credit is 50%.

WAD lab and project submissions permit an automatic 24-hour grace period with a 10% penalty deduction. Submissions delayed past 48 hours receive zero marks. All code is checked for originality using automated AST and MOSS analysis.

title: DCN & Machine Learning (ML) Laboratory Regulations & Guidelines

chunks.sectionTitle: Machine Learning (ML) Lab Timetable and GPU Access
chunks.content: Machine Learning (ML) is instructed by Prof. DT. Theory classes are in Room 201/402. Lab sessions: Batch B1 on Tuesdays 02:10 PM - 04:00 PM in Lab 3A; Batch B2 on Mondays 11:10 AM - 01:00 PM in Lab 5C; Batch B3 on Mondays 02:10 PM - 04:00 PM in Lab 3A. Dedicated GPU workstations are allocated for neural networks and classification models.

chunks.sectionTitle: Data Communication & Networks (DCN) Lab & Wireshark Rules
chunks.content: Data Communication and Networks (DCN) is instructed by Prof. MSG in Room 402. Lab practicals: Batch B1 on Wednesdays 11:10 AM - 01:00 PM in Lab 2C; Batch B2 on Mondays 02:10 PM - 04:00 PM in Lab 2C; Batch B3 on Mondays 11:10 AM - 01:00 PM in Lab 2C. Wireshark packet capturing must strictly follow university firewall safety policies.

System Software (SS) is taught by Prof. VP in Room 402, with lab practicals in Lab MP (Microprocessor/Systems Lab). VLSI Design is instructed by Prof. PRG in Room 303B and Lab MP. Students must maintain lab observation logbooks signed weekly by the instructor.

The official academic timetable took effect on 05/08/2026. Classes run daily Monday through Friday from 09:10 AM to 06:00 PM with common lunch break from 01:10 PM to 02:00 PM. Sports and recreational activities are scheduled on Mondays from 05:10 PM to 06:00 PM.

Midterm assessments for WAD, ML, DCN, SS, DMBI, and VLSI take place from October 12 to October 20, 2026 in Examination Block 402 and 201. Final Examination week spans from December 7 to December 18, 2026. Seating allocations will be released by the Registrar 7 days prior.

chunks.sectionTitle: Medical Certificate Protocol and Special Exam Window
chunks.content: Students missing assessments due to genuine illness or emergency must submit a university health certificate within 48 hours to the department head. Special supplementary exams will be conducted on December 21-22, 2026.
